config.title: TanStack Query Basics

intro.title: TanStack Query Basics
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React app that fetches and displays a list of users from a mock API. You will learn the core concept of server-state management using TanStack Query, which simplifies data fetching, caching, and synchronization. The main technologies involved are React with TypeScript (TSX) and the TanStack Query library, including hooks like useQuery. By the end, you'll understand how to efficiently load and handle data in your components without manual state management.
intro.usecase: TanStack Query is essential for building modern data-driven applications like e-commerce dashboards that display real-time sales analytics, social media feeds that update with new posts, and collaborative tools that sync user activity across devices. Developers use it to implement product filtering interfaces that fetch and cache category data, user profile panels that load and update personal information, and notification systems that poll for new alerts. This pattern eliminates manual loading states and error handling boilerplate while ensuring users always see fresh data without unnecessary network requests.

objectives: Initialize a TanStack Query client and wrap your React application with the QueryClientProvider
Configure a custom query hook using useQuery to fetch data from an API endpoint
Implement loading and error states in your UI based on TanStack Query's status indicators
Manipulate query data by implementing refetching mechanisms in response to user actions
Construct a component that displays fetched data with proper TypeScript type annotations
Integrate TanStack Query's caching behavior by configuring query options like staleTime
Update component state in coordination with TanStack Query's data synchronization

steps.title: Import React, TanStack Query, and fetch API dependencies
steps.instruction: Import React, QueryClient, QueryClientProvider, and useQuery from '@tanstack/react-query', and also import the fetch function for making API calls.
steps.hint: You'll need to write import statements for React and the TanStack Query packages. The fetch function is globally available in browsers, but for TypeScript compatibility, you can import it from a type definition.
steps.seedCode: // Import React, TanStack Query, and fetch API dependencies here
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary imports for React, TanStack Query, and the fetch function are added to the file.
successCriteria: React, QueryClient, QueryClientProvider, useQuery, and fetch are all imported correctly.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some dependencies, but check if you're missing any from the list: React, QueryClient, QueryClientProvider, useQuery, and fetch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are not correct. Make sure to import React, QueryClient, QueryClientProvider, and useQuery from '@tanstack/react-query', and also import the fetch function.

steps.title: Create a QueryClient instance
steps.instruction: Create a new QueryClient instance outside the component to be used throughout the application. Name it 'queryClient'.
steps.hint: Use the QueryClient constructor from '@tanstack/react-query' to create a new instance.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating an instance of a class
const httpClient = new HttpClient();
steps.expectedOutcome: A QueryClient instance named 'queryClient' is created outside the component, ready to be used for managing queries and caching.
successCriteria: A QueryClient instance named 'queryClient' is created using the QueryClient constructor.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're creating a new QueryClient instance with the correct syntax and naming it 'queryClient'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The QueryClient instance wasn't created correctly. Remember to use the QueryClient constructor from '@tanstack/react-query' and name it 'queryClient'.

steps.title: Define the main App component
steps.instruction: Define a functional App component that returns a basic container element. The component should return a <div> with the text 'TanStack Query Basics' inside an <h1> heading.
steps.hint: Inside the App component, return JSX that includes a <div> wrapping an <h1> element with the specified text.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now returns a <div> containing an <h1> with the text 'TanStack Query Basics'.
successCriteria: The App component is defined and returns a <div> with an <h1> containing the text 'TanStack Query Basics'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the component doesn't yet return the expected JSX. Make sure it returns a <div> with an <h1> containing 'TanStack Query Basics'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component is not defined correctly. It should return a <div> with an <h1> containing 'TanStack Query Basics'.

steps.title: Wrap the app with QueryClientProvider
steps.instruction: Wrap the App component's return statement with QueryClientProvider and pass the QueryClient instance as a prop.
steps.hint: Import QueryClientProvider from '@tanstack/react-query' and use it as a wrapper element around your App component's content.
steps.analogousExample:
// Wrapping a component with a provider
<QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
  <App />
</QueryClientProvider>
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is wrapped with QueryClientProvider, making the QueryClient instance available to all child components.
successCriteria: QueryClientProvider is imported and wraps the App component's return statement, with the client prop set to the queryClient instance.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've imported QueryClientProvider and wrapped the App component's return statement with it, passing the queryClient instance as the client prop.
steps.feedbackWrong: The app is not properly wrapped with QueryClientProvider. Check that you've imported QueryClientProvider and used it to wrap your App component's content with the client prop set to queryClient.

steps.title: Define a fetch function for API data
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, define an async function named 'fetchPosts' that uses fetch to retrieve data from 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts' and returns the parsed JSON.
steps.hint: Use the fetch API inside an async function. Remember to await the fetch call and the .json() method to get the data.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an async fetchPosts function defined inside the App component, ready to be used with TanStack Query.
successCriteria: The fetchPosts function is defined inside the App component, uses fetch with the correct URL, and returns the parsed JSON data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is async, uses the correct URL, and returns the parsed JSON data from the fetch call.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchPosts function isn't defined correctly. Check that it's an async function inside the App component that fetches from the URL and returns the parsed JSON.

steps.title: Create a custom hook to fetch posts using useQuery
steps.instruction: Create a custom hook named 'usePosts' that uses the useQuery hook to fetch posts data. The hook should define a QueryKey, use the fetchPosts function, and include TypeScript interfaces for the post data structure.
steps.hint: Start by defining an interface for the Post type, then create a function that returns the result of useQuery with appropriate configuration.
steps.expectedOutcome: A custom hook named 'usePosts' that properly uses useQuery with TypeScript types for fetching posts data.
successCriteria: The usePosts hook is defined, includes a Post interface, uses useQuery with a queryKey and queryFn, and returns the query result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your hook includes: 1) A Post interface, 2) The useQuery hook with queryKey and queryFn, 3) Proper return type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook isn't quite right. Remember to create a function named 'usePosts' that returns a useQuery call with a queryKey and queryFn, and includes TypeScript interfaces.

steps.title: Add a component to display fetched posts
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named Posts that uses the custom hook to fetch posts and returns a loading state, error state, and the list of posts.
steps.hint: Define a component that calls the custom hook and conditionally renders different UI based on the query status.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Posts component is defined that uses the custom hook and handles loading, error, and success states.
successCriteria: Posts component is defined, uses the custom hook, and returns conditional JSX for loading, error, and data states.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined the Posts component, but it's missing some required conditional rendering logic.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Posts component is not defined correctly or doesn't use the custom hook properly.

steps.title: Integrate the Posts component into the App
steps.instruction: Inside the App component's return statement, add the Posts component so it renders within the QueryClientProvider wrapper.
steps.hint: Place the Posts component as a child element inside the QueryClientProvider tags.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now renders the Posts component inside the QueryClientProvider, enabling the posts data to be displayed.
successCriteria: Posts component is rendered inside QueryClientProvider in App's return statement
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the Posts component is placed inside the QueryClientProvider tags in the App's return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Posts component needs to be rendered inside the QueryClientProvider in the App component's return statement.

steps.title: Add a refetch button to manually trigger data fetching
steps.instruction: In the Posts component, add a button element that calls the refetch function from the useQuery result when clicked.
steps.hint: The useQuery hook returns an object containing a refetch function. Add a button with an onClick handler that calls this function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Button that triggers a function
<button onClick={() => refetch()}>Refresh Data</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The Posts component will include a button that, when clicked, manually triggers a refetch of the posts data using TanStack Query's refetch function.
successCriteria: A button element is added to the Posts component with an onClick handler that calls the refetch function from the useQuery result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it calls the refetch function from useQuery when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured to trigger data refetching. Check that it calls the refetch function from useQuery.

steps.title: Display query status and timestamp
steps.instruction: Inside the Posts component, add a paragraph that displays the query's status and the timestamp of the last successful fetch using the dataUpdatedAt property from the query result.
steps.hint: Access the status and dataUpdatedAt properties from the query result object returned by useQuery. Format the timestamp using new Date().toLocaleString().
steps.expectedOutcome: The Posts component will show the current query status (loading, error, or success) and the time when the data was last successfully fetched.
successCriteria: The Posts component includes a paragraph that displays both the query status and formatted timestamp from dataUpdatedAt.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying both the status and the formatted timestamp from dataUpdatedAt.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Posts component should display the query status and last fetched timestamp. Check that you're accessing the correct properties from the query result.
